title: the thing that's yours to do
hook: a warrior puts down his bow and says he no longer knows what's right
carry: do the thing that's yours to do

segments.voice: Yesterday: puja. Your line was attention is an offering. Today, the word at the center of the Bhagavad Gita.

The Bhagavad Gita opens on a battlefield. A warrior named Arjuna asks his charioteer to drive him out between the two armies, and he sees his own family on the other side: teachers, uncles, cousins. His bow slips from his hand and he sits down in the chariot. The word he reaches for, to say what he's lost, is today's word.

Dharma gets translated as duty, law or religion, and each of those catches only a piece. It comes from a Sanskrit root meaning to hold, or to support. Dharma is what holds things up: teachers say the dharma of fire is to burn and the dharma of water is to flow. It's what a thing is for, the part it holds in the whole. In the Gita's second chapter, Arjuna says his mind is confused about dharma, and he asks his charioteer, Krishna, to teach him. The rest of the Gita is that teaching. One line from the third chapter shows where it starts: better your own dharma, even done imperfectly, than someone else's done well. Your own dharma is svadharma. So dharma isn't only rules handed down. It's also a question: what is mine to do here? Arjuna isn't missing information. He's lost the thread of what's his to do.
screen: `DHARMA — WHAT HOLDS THINGS UP.` · `I AM YOUR STUDENT. TEACH ME.` · `YOUR OWN, EVEN IMPERFECTLY.` · `WHAT IS MINE TO DO HERE?`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, bring to mind one thing you've been putting off. On the second, ask it once, silently: what's mine to do here? On the third, let the question go. No plan needed yet.
Dharma. From a root meaning to hold: what holds things up, and your share of the holding. Ninth word.
Your line: do the thing that's yours to do. It's the question the whole Gita answers, and this path comes back to it. Day nine.

screen: `DAY 9 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE ONE BEHIND YOUR EYES.`

howItsDone: Hindus speak of dharma as right action and the order that holds life together, and also of svadharma, one's own duty in a given place and stage of life; the Bhagavad Gita is read and recited as a guide to it.

story.title: the dog at heaven's gate
story.text: At the very end of the Mahabharata, the five Pandava brothers and Draupadi walk toward the Himalayas, and one by one they fall. Only the eldest, Yudhishthira, is left, with a dog that has followed him the whole way. The god Indra arrives in a chariot to carry him to heaven, but says the dog can't come. Yudhishthira refuses. He won't abandon someone who stayed loyal to him, not even for heaven. Then the dog changes shape. It was Dharma himself, testing him, and Yudhishthira had passed.
